newsitem.title: south africa: Shroud of secrecy covers Zaire peace bid.
newsitem.headline: Shroud of secrecy covers Zaire peace bid.

text.p: Zaire's warring parties inched toward their first talks on Thursday as their South African hosts sought to protect the delicate process behind a shroud of secrecy.
Parks Mankahlana, spokesman for President Nelson Mandela, confirmed to Reuters the breakthrough peace initiative was on track, but added: "We are not releasing any details."

A government source said Deputy President Thabo Mbeki was leading a series of meetings in his Cape Town office aiming to bring Zairean rebel leader Laurent Kabila and Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko's nephew and chief security adviser, Ngbanda Nzambo Ko Ayumba, together later on Thursday.
The two sides have not met since fighting erupted in Zaire when ethnic Tutsi rebels took up arms in October.

A U.S. embassy official confirmed Assistant-Secretary of State for African Affairs, George Moose, and U.S. National Security Council Senior Director for Africa, Susan Rice, were in Cape Town to bolster the process.
"The U.S. is prepared to help this effort if we can...We welcome any serious effort to achieve this goal," Rice said.

South African Director General of Foreign Affairs Rusty Evans, who said on Wednesday Kabila was in the country, stepped back on Thursday, saying he could not confirm or deny his presence or that of any other rebel representative.
Evans declined to detail contacts that led to the talks, saying: "There is a great reluctance on both sides to acknowledge that they are willing to negotiate."

Mandela said on Wednesday South Africa would send a plane for Kabila, and military sources said he was believed to have been on an aircraft that landed at a Cape Town air force base from Rwanda shortly before dawn.
Evans said South Africa's only role would be to facilitate a first meeting between the government of the ailing Mobutu and the rebels.
"We are more than willing and very pleased to provide a venue for them to meet. How they meet, how they conduct their meeting and what they choose to say about it is for them to decide," he said.
Evans called presumptuous claims by diplomats that Mandela had undermined the fledgling initiative by revealing the plan while responding to questions after a regional summit.
Zaire's rebel forces, holding territory along the border with Rwanda, Burundi and Uganda, have faced a renewed government offensive since Monday.

According to Mandela, the peace proposal for Zaire under discussion would be separate from a U.N. call earlier this week for an immediate ceasefire and Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni's call for a truce leading to democratic elections.

A South African diplomatic source said there was a framework agreement on the table, setting out a strategy to resolve the escalating conflict. "We have a problem with expectations that are being raised...this is going to be a long process," he said.

Mandela said Mobutu and Kabila had jointly asked to be allowed to meet in South Africa, but a diplomatic source told Reuters the initiative had come from the Zairean government, which previously had refused to meet the rebels.
The source said the idea was put to Mbeki on Sunday and was followed up on Monday in talks between Mbeki and visiting U.S. Vice President Al Gore, who promoted the proposal.
South African government sources say Mandela seeks to manage the initiative as an African effort and would prefer to exclude the United States and France.
